lessons.title: Agent fundamentals: tools, state, budgets and stopping
lessons.summary: Build and defend a bounded tool-using agent: agent vs workflow, validated tool schemas, run state, stop conditions, error feedback and loop detection.
keyPoints: An agent lets the model choose the next step in a loop; a workflow keeps control flow in your code. Default to a workflow and add agency only where the path depends on discoveries.
The model only emits requests. Your code validates arguments against a strict schema, authorises against the user's permissions, then executes. That boundary is where safety lives.
Anything that must be guaranteed (step, token and time budgets, repeat detection) lives in code, never only in the prompt.
Return validation and tool errors to the model as precise observations; retry transient failures inside the tool layer; circuit-break after consecutive errors.
Check budgets before running tools from the reply that exceeded them, and give each stop reason a distinct status you can monitor.
Control side effects with least privilege, dry-run, idempotency keys, caps on the action and approval for irreversible steps.
Test control flow deterministically with a scripted fake model; measure real-model quality separately on an eval set.

check.q: Why should the token budget be checked before executing the tool calls in a model reply?
options: Tool calls are cheaper than model calls, so order does not matter
A reply that exceeds the budget may still contain a dangerous or expensive tool call that would otherwise run
Providers reject requests that exceed the budget
It makes the model answer faster
check.why: If the budget check runs after tools execute, the final over-budget reply can still trigger a side effect. Checking first guarantees nothing runs once the limit is crossed.

check.q: Which loop-detection key best catches a model repeating the same call with reordered JSON keys?
options: Tool name only
The raw argument string as the model wrote it
A counter on (tool name, canonical JSON of args with sorted keys), tripping on the third identical call
The step number modulo 3
check.why: Canonicalising arguments (sorted keys) makes semantically identical calls collide. Tool name alone is too coarse and would block legitimate repeated use with different args.

check.q: A tool times out on a write that may have partially succeeded. What is the safest retry design?
options: Let the model retry it in the next step
Retry in the tool layer with an idempotency key so a repeat cannot duplicate the effect
Never retry any tool
Retry immediately in a tight loop until it works
check.why: Retrying a non-idempotent write can duplicate its effect. An idempotency key makes the retry safe, and doing it in the tool layer avoids spending model steps on network blips.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Agent vs workflow, tool schema, state, stopping conditions, error handling.
> **Prerequisites:** Prompting and API patterns week.
> **Estimated time:** 45 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Bounded tool-using agent.

## What an agent is, in one sentence

An **agent** is a program in which a language model decides, at run time, which action to take next (usually which tool to call) based on what it has observed so far, and the loop ends when the model says it is done or a limit stops it. A **workflow** is a program in which *your code* decides the path and the model only fills in steps along it.

That one distinction (who controls the next step) drives every design decision this week. This lesson covers the fundamentals; the GenAI End to End course, chapter 4 (agents and tools) goes deeper on frameworks and patterns, so see the GenAI End to End course, chapter 4 for those. Here you build the core loop yourself and learn to defend it.

## Agent vs deterministic workflow

| | Workflow (prompt chain, router, parallel fan-out) | Agent (model-directed loop) |
|---|---|---|
| Who picks the next step | Your code | The model |
| Number of model calls | Fixed or bounded by the graph | Variable, unbounded without limits |
| Latency | Predictable | Long-tailed (one bad run takes 10x the median) |
| Cost per request | Predictable | Long-tailed |
| Testability | Each step testable, paths enumerable | Trajectories vary run to run |
| Failure shape | A step returns bad output | Wrong tool, wrong order, loops, drift |
| Best for | Tasks whose steps you can write down | Open-ended tasks where steps depend on what you find |

A useful rule from Anthropic's "Building effective agents" essay: start with the simplest thing (one well-prompted call, then a workflow) and add agency only when the task genuinely cannot be decomposed ahead of time. Examples:

- "Classify this ticket, then draft a reply from a template": workflow. Steps are known.
- "Summarise 40 documents": workflow (map-reduce). Fan-out is known.
- "Investigate why this order is stuck and fix it if safe": agent. You do not know in advance which systems you will need to look at.

**When it breaks:** teams reach for an agent because it demos well, then spend months fighting variance that a 3-step workflow would not have had. If you can draw the flowchart before running the task, you probably want a workflow.

## The agent loop

```
messages = [user task]
repeat:
    reply = model(messages, tool_schemas)
    if reply has no tool calls: return reply.text        # model decided it is done
    for each tool call:
        validate args against the tool's schema
        run the tool (or return an error string)
        append the observation to messages
    check budgets (steps, tokens, time, repeats)
```

Everything else (planning, memory, reflection, multi-agent) is a variation on this loop. Two things to notice:

1. The model never executes anything. It emits a *request* (tool name plus JSON arguments). Your code validates, authorises and runs it. That boundary is where you put every safety control.
2. The model only knows about the world through the message list. "State" is whatever you put back into that list or into a store your tools can read.

## Tool schemas: the contract

The model learns a tool only through its **name, description and parameter schema** (JSON Schema in most provider APIs; check provider docs for exact field names). That makes the schema both documentation and the first validation layer.

Good tool design:

- **Narrow and named by intent.** `get_order_status(order_id)` beats `run_sql(query)`. A narrow tool can be reasoned about, authorised and tested; a general one cannot.
- **Strict schemas.** Types, enums, `minimum`/`maximum`, `required`, `additionalProperties: false`. Every constraint you encode is a class of bad call you reject for free.
- **Descriptions say when *not* to use it.** "Looks up one order by id. Do not use for searching by customer name."
- **Small, bounded outputs.** Return the fields needed, truncate long text, paginate. A 50 KB tool result is paid for on every later step because it stays in the context.
- **Mark side effects.** Separate read tools from write tools in your own registry. Reads can retry freely; writes need idempotency keys, dry-run modes and often approval (next week).

**Never trust the arguments even though a model produced them.** The model is a function of its context, and the context may contain attacker text. Validate every call exactly as you would validate an HTTP request body, then authorise it against the *user's* permissions, not the agent's.

## State

There are three kinds of state in an agent run:

| State | Where it lives | Example | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conversation / scratchpad | The message list | Prior tool calls and results | Grows every step; cost and distraction |
| Run state | Your code | Step count, tokens used, seen call signatures, error streak | If it lives only in the model's head, you cannot enforce limits |
| External state | DB, files, APIs | The order you refunded | Side effects survive the run, so retries can duplicate them |

The key discipline: **anything you need to enforce must live in code, not in the prompt.** "Do not call more than 5 tools" in a system prompt is a request. `max_steps = 5` in the loop is a guarantee.

For longer runs you also need to control context growth: truncate tool outputs, summarise old turns, or drop results that are no longer needed. Each step re-sends the whole history, so cost grows roughly quadratically with step count if outputs are large.

### Worked arithmetic: why step limits matter

Suppose the system prompt plus tool schemas are 1,500 tokens, each step adds 600 tokens (call plus result), and the model emits 100 tokens per step. Input tokens at step *n* are about 1,500 + 600 *(n-1).

- 5 steps: input tokens per step are 1,500, 2,100, 2,700, 3,300 and 3,900, which sum to 13,500, plus 500 output tokens.
- 20 steps: inputs sum = 20 * 1,500 + 600 * (0+1+...+19) = 30,000 + 600 * 190 = 144,000 input tokens.

Four times the steps costs about 10.7 times the input tokens. (Provider prompt caching can discount repeated prefixes substantially; this is the uncached worst case. Prices change, so multiply by the current price per million tokens from the provider docs.) A runaway loop is therefore a *cost* bug as much as a correctness bug.

## Stopping conditions

An agent can stop for good reasons and bad reasons. Make every one explicit and return a distinct status so you can monitor it.

| Status | Trigger | What the caller does |
|---|---|---|
| `done` | Model returns an answer with no tool calls | Return it (after output validation) |
| `max_steps` | Step counter hits the cap | Return partial result or escalate to a human |
| `token_budget` | Cumulative tokens exceed budget | Stop *before* running more tools |
| `timeout` | Wall clock exceeded | Same; make the clock injectable for tests |
| `loop_detected` | Same tool plus same args repeated | Stop; log the signature |
| `too_many_errors` | N consecutive tool failures | Circuit breaker; escalate |

Two subtleties: check budgets **before** executing tool calls from a reply that already blew the budget (otherwise the last expensive or dangerous action still happens), and treat a *natural* stop with suspicion in high-stakes flows: "done" is the model's claim, not a verified fact. Validate the output (schema, citations, a postcondition check such as "refund row exists").

## Error handling

Tool failures are normal. Three layers:

1. **Return errors to the model as observations**, with enough detail to self-correct: `ERROR: invalid arguments: $.order_id: expected string, got integer`. Models are often good at fixing a call when told precisely what was wrong. Do not return stack traces or internal hostnames.
2. **Retry transient failures in the tool layer, not via the model.** Timeouts and 429/5xx get exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, inside the tool wrapper. The model should not burn a step (and tokens) to retry a network blip. Never blindly retry non-idempotent writes.
3. **Circuit-break.** After N consecutive failures, stop and escalate rather than letting the model flail. Retrying 4xx validation errors unchanged is pointless; honour `Retry-After` for 429.

## Loop detection

Models loop in two ways: **identical repeats** (same tool, same arguments, because the observation did not change their mind) and **oscillation** (A, B, A, B). The cheap defence is a counter keyed by `(tool name, canonical JSON of args)`; the third identical call stops the run. Oscillation shows up as the same pair of signatures repeating; extend the key to a window if you need it. Also useful: stop when the last K observations are identical, and show the model a note ("this call returned the same result twice") before you hard-stop.

## Preventing dangerous side effects

Think in layers, outermost first:

- **Least privilege:** the tool's credentials can do only what that tool needs (read-only DB role for lookup tools).
- **Dry run:** write tools return "would do X" until a flag enables them. Great for tests and shadow mode.
- **Idempotency keys:** a retried refund must not refund twice.
- **Approval gates:** a human confirms irreversible or high-value actions (next week).
- **Budget caps on the action itself:** refund at most 50 currency units without approval.
- **Audit log:** who (user), which agent run, which tool, which args, what result.

## Decision guide

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| One-shot transformation or Q&A | Single call |
| Fixed sequence of steps | Prompt chain / workflow |
| Fixed set of branches by input type | Router + workflows |
| Open-ended investigation, unknown number of lookups | Bounded agent |
| Needs durable pause/resume, approvals, branching | Stateful graph (next week) |
| High-stakes irreversible actions | Agent proposes, human or deterministic code disposes |

## Trade-offs

- **Quality vs latency/cost:** more steps can find more, but each step adds latency (seconds) and tokens. Set budgets from measurement, not hope.
- **Flexibility vs testability:** the more the model decides, the more trajectories you must evaluate.
- **Generic vs narrow tools:** narrow tools are safer and more reliable; generic ones cover more cases and invite misuse.
- **Autonomy vs safety:** every removed approval gate is an accepted risk; make it a conscious one.

## Common failure modes

1. **Runaway loop:** repeated calls with no progress (fix: caps, signature counter).
2. **Wrong tool or hallucinated tool/arg:** (fix: strict schemas, unknown-tool errors, fewer and clearer tools).
3. **Context bloat:** huge tool outputs crowd out instructions (fix: truncate, summarise).
4. **Premature "done":** model answers without checking (fix: required postcondition checks, output validation).
5. **Duplicate side effects on retry:** (fix: idempotency keys).
6. **Silent partial failure:** the run stops at `max_steps` and the caller treats the empty result as success (fix: distinct statuses, alerts).

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The 'agent' was an unbounded loop that called search, then browse, then search again until the timeout. There was no tool schema, no token or step budget, and no stop condition besides the provider killing the request. State was the raw transcript. A calculator tool accepted a string and `eval`'d it. When asked the difference between an agent and a workflow the candidate said 'agents are smarter'.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'When is a workflow the better design?' Outline: the steps are known, the tools are few, and you want a testable path. Follow-up: 'How do you stop a runaway agent?' Answer: max steps, max tokens, a deny list of tools after N failures, and a human checkpoint before side effects.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a second agent framework and an open-ended browse tool. Keep a schema, a budget, a stop rule, and one tool you can stub in a test.

parts.label: Worked example
parts.body:
## What you are building

A **bounded tool-using agent** in about 150 lines of dependency-free Python, plus tests that run without any API key. The proof artifact for the week is: the loop, a validated tool registry, hard budgets, loop detection, error-to-model feedback, a dry-run mode for writes, and a pytest suite driven by a **scripted fake model**.

Why a fake model? Real models are non-deterministic, slow and cost money, and you cannot write a test like "the agent stops on the third identical call" against one. The agent's *control flow* is ordinary code, so test it with ordinary determinism: the fake model returns a pre-written list of replies, and the tests assert on what the loop did with them.

Layout (run all of it in one folder):

```
tools.py        # validate(), Tool, Registry, ToolError
agent.py        # Budget, Agent.run(), RunResult
test_agent.py   # pytest tests with ScriptedModel
```

## Walkthrough of `tools.py`

- `validate(value, schema)` is a tiny JSON-Schema-style validator that returns a **list of error strings** such as `$.a: expected integer, got str`. Returning all problems at once lets the model fix everything in one retry. In production you would normally use the `jsonschema` or `pydantic` package; writing a mini version once shows exactly what a schema check does. Note the explicit `bool` rejection: in Python `True` is an `int`, which would otherwise sneak through an `integer` field.
- `Tool` has a `writes` flag. `Registry.call` does, in order: unknown-tool check, schema validation, dry-run short-circuit for writes, execute inside `try/except`, truncate the result. Every failure becomes a `ToolError` with a message safe to show the model. The model never sees a stack trace.
- `Registry.specs()` is what you send to the provider as the tool list. Provider payload shapes differ slightly (field names for the schema key, for example); adapt in one place and check the provider docs.

## Walkthrough of `agent.py`

- `Budget` holds **all** limits in one frozen dataclass: steps, tokens, seconds, consecutive errors, identical calls. Defaults are conservative; tune them from traces.
- `Agent.run` keeps run state (`tokens`, `seen`, `consecutive_errors`) in local variables, not in the prompt, so limits are guarantees.
- The token check happens **right after the model call and before any tool runs**. If the reply pushed you over budget, a dangerous tool call in that same reply is never executed. A test pins this behaviour.
- Loop detection uses `(tool name, json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True))` as the signature, so `{"a":1,"b":2}` and `{"b":2,"a":1}` count as the same call. With `max_identical_calls=2` the third identical call stops the run.
- Errors become observations (`ERROR: ...`) and the loop continues, unless `max_consecutive_errors` is hit (circuit breaker).
- The clock is injected (`clock=time.monotonic` by default) so the timeout test does not sleep.
- `RunResult.trace` is a list of events. It is the seed of the observability story in the reliability week: each step, tool name, ok/failed, tokens.

## Walkthrough of `test_agent.py`

| Test | Behaviour pinned |
|---|---|
| `test_happy_path_returns_answer` | Tool result is appended as a `tool` message and the run ends with `done` |
| `test_invalid_args_are_fed_back_and_model_can_recover` | Validation errors reach the model verbatim and a corrected call succeeds |
| `test_unknown_tool_is_an_error_observation_not_a_crash` | Hallucinated tool names do not raise |
| `test_tool_exception_becomes_error_observation` | A crashing tool is converted to text |
| `test_max_steps_stops_a_model_that_never_finishes` | Hard step cap, even if every call is different |
| `test_identical_calls_are_detected_as_a_loop` | Third identical call stops with `loop_detected` at step 3 |
| `test_token_budget_stops_before_running_the_tool` | Over-budget reply never triggers a side effect |
| `test_wall_clock_budget_uses_injected_clock` | Timeout without sleeping |
| `test_consecutive_errors_trip_the_circuit_breaker` | N failures in a row stop the run |
| `test_dry_run_blocks_write_tools` | Write tool body never runs in dry run |
| `test_validator_rejects_bool_as_integer_and_extra_keys` | Validator edge cases |

Run it with `pytest -q`. The suite finishes in milliseconds and needs no network.

## Connecting a real model

The agent only needs a callable `model(messages, tools) -> ModelReply`. To use a provider, write an adapter that (1) converts your `messages` and `tools` into the provider's request format, (2) calls the SDK, and (3) maps the response into `ModelReply(text, tool_calls, tokens)` using the usage numbers the API returns. Keep the adapter thin and test it separately with recorded responses. Check the provider's tool-use docs for current message and field names rather than copying them from memory.

## Exercises to reach "proof artifact" level

1. Add a **window-based oscillation detector** (A, B, A, B) and a test with a scripted model that alternates.
2. Add **`max_result_chars` per tool** and a test showing a 10,000-character result is truncated with a marker.
3. Add an **idempotency key** to a write tool (`refund`) and test that a repeated call with the same key performs one side effect.
4. Write an **`approval` hook** that the registry consults for `writes=True` tools; return `"ERROR: approval denied"` when it says no. (Next week turns this into a real interrupt.)
5. Add a **trace dump** to JSON and assert that a `loop_detected` run's trace ends with the right stop event.

## What to say about this in an interview

"I built a framework-free agent loop first so I understand what frameworks hide: a tool registry with schema validation, budgets enforced in code, loop detection, errors fed back to the model, and a dry-run mode. I tested the control flow with a scripted fake model, so the tests are deterministic. I have not evaluated it against a real model's task success; that needs a task set, which is the reliability-week artifact." That sentence is honest, specific and invites the right follow-ups.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The 'agent' was an unbounded loop that called search, then browse, then search again until the timeout. There was no tool schema, no token or step budget, and no stop condition besides the provider killing the request. State was the raw transcript. A calculator tool accepted a string and `eval`'d it. When asked the difference between an agent and a workflow the candidate said 'agents are smarter'.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'When is a workflow the better design?' Outline: the steps are known, the tools are few, and you want a testable path. Follow-up: 'How do you stop a runaway agent?' Answer: max steps, max tokens, a deny list of tools after N failures, and a human checkpoint before side effects.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut a second agent framework and an open-ended browse tool. Keep a schema, a budget, a stop rule, and one tool you can stub in a test.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
Use the same shape every time: **Define, Mechanism, Decision, Trade-off, Evidence.** Say the 60-90 second version out loud, then rehearse the follow-ups.

## Q1. What distinguishes an agent from a deterministic workflow?

**Define:** In a workflow my code decides the sequence of steps and the model fills in content; in an agent the model decides the next step at run time, in a loop, until it stops or a limit stops it.

**Mechanism:** An agent loop sends messages and tool schemas to the model. If the reply contains tool calls, my code validates and runs them, appends the observations, and calls the model again. If it contains plain text, the loop ends. A workflow has the control flow in code: classify, then retrieve, then draft, with branches I wrote.

**Decision:** I use a workflow when I can draw the flowchart in advance, because it is cheaper, faster, predictable and easier to test. I use a bounded agent when the number and order of lookups depends on what earlier steps find, such as investigating a stuck order. Often the answer is a workflow with one agentic step inside it.

**Trade-off:** Agents buy flexibility and pay with variance in latency, cost and path, and with a bigger test surface. Workflows are rigid but each step can be evaluated alone.

**Evidence:** In my own code I wrote the loop without a framework and tested the control flow with a scripted fake model. If I had not, I would say: I understand the distinction and would validate it by running the same task set through both designs and comparing success rate, p95 latency and cost per task.

**Failure mode to mention:** picking an agent for a fixed task and then fighting variance that a three-step workflow would not have.

**60-90 second version:** "The difference is who controls the next step. In a workflow, my code does: step one, step two, branch on this condition, and the model is just a component producing text or structured output at each step. In an agent, the model chooses the next action each turn, usually a tool call, my code runs it, feeds back the result, and it loops until the model answers or I hit a limit. So agents handle open-ended tasks where I cannot predict the steps, but I pay in variance: more model calls, longer tail latency, harder tests. I default to a workflow, and add agency only where the task really needs it, with budgets so the loop is bounded. For example, ticket classification and drafting is a workflow; investigating why an order is stuck across several systems is a bounded agent."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Is a router an agent?* Usually no. A router picks among predefined paths once; it does not loop. The line blurs when the router is re-invoked after each step.
- *Is ReAct the same thing?* ReAct is a prompting pattern of interleaving reasoning and actions; modern tool-calling APIs implement the action half natively. The loop above is the same shape.
- *Can an agent be deterministic?* Not strictly; temperature 0 reduces but does not eliminate variance, and tool outputs change. You make behaviour *bounded and testable*, not deterministic.

## Q2. How do tool schemas, validation, retries, state and stop conditions work together?

**Define:** They are the five parts of the contract between a non-deterministic model and deterministic systems: the schema says what a call may look like, validation enforces it, retries and error feedback handle failures, state records what happened, and stop conditions bound the run.

**Mechanism:** The model sees tool names, descriptions and JSON Schemas. When it emits a call, my code validates the arguments against the schema and returns every violation as an error observation if invalid, so the model can fix it. If valid, I authorise against the user's permissions and execute; transient failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) are retried inside the tool wrapper with backoff and a cap, not by spending a model step. Run state (step count, tokens, seen call signatures, error streak) lives in my code. After each step I check stop conditions: done, max steps, token budget, wall clock, repeated call, consecutive errors. Each stop has its own status.

**Decision:** Put anything that must be guaranteed in code, not in the prompt. Use model-visible feedback for errors the model can fix (bad args), and code-level retries for errors it cannot (network).

**Trade-off:** Strict schemas reject more bad calls but increase early-step errors if descriptions are poor; verbose error messages help self-correction but can leak internals if you are careless. More retries improve availability and cost latency and money.

**Evidence:** I tested each rule with a scripted model: invalid args come back as text and a corrected call succeeds, the token budget stops before the tool body runs, the third identical call trips loop detection. If asked for production evidence, I would say what I measured on real runs: the distribution of stop statuses, which tells me whether limits are too tight or the prompt is weak.

**Failure mode to mention:** retrying a non-idempotent write after a timeout and performing it twice. Fix with idempotency keys.

**60-90 second version:** "I think of it as a contract. The schema tells the model what a valid call looks like. Validation enforces that, because the arguments are untrusted: they came from a model whose context might contain attacker text. If validation fails, I return all the errors as an observation so the model can correct itself. If a tool fails transiently, the tool layer retries with backoff, so the model does not waste a step. Run state, meaning steps, tokens, time, and a counter of identical calls, lives in code, because prompts are requests and code is a guarantee. And I have explicit stop conditions with distinct statuses: done, max steps, token budget, timeout, loop detected, too many errors. One detail I care about is checking the budget before executing the tools in the reply that exceeded it."

**Follow-ups:**
- *What goes in the error message?* Which field, what was expected, what was received; no stack traces, hostnames or secrets.
- *Where do you put authorisation?* In the tool wrapper, checked against the end user's identity. The agent's credentials should not be broader than the user's.
- *How do you handle partial progress when you stop?* Return what was gathered with the status, and either escalate or let the user continue; never present a `max_steps` result as a complete answer.

## Q3. How do you prevent runaway loops, excessive tool calls and dangerous side effects?

**Define:** Bound the run with hard budgets enforced in code, detect repetition, and make every side effect safe to retry, reversible, or gated.

**Mechanism:** Four layers. (1) Budgets: max steps, max cumulative tokens, wall-clock timeout, per-run tool-call cap, checked each iteration. (2) Detection: a counter on (tool, canonical args) catches identical repeats; a short window catches A-B-A-B; consecutive-error circuit breaker. (3) Side-effect control: read tools separated from write tools, least-privilege credentials, dry-run mode, idempotency keys, caps on the action itself (refund limit), and approval for irreversible actions. (4) Observability: a trace per run and alerts on stop statuses other than done.

**Decision:** Always on: budgets and detection. Add approval gates in proportion to blast radius: reads are free, reversible writes get logged, irreversible or high-value writes get a human.

**Trade-off:** Tight budgets cut off legitimate long tasks; loose budgets cost money in the bad case. Approvals add latency and annoy users if overused, so reserve them for risk.

**Evidence:** I wrote tests for each stop reason. To tune limits on a real system I would look at the distribution of steps and tokens for successful runs and set the cap at a high percentile plus margin, then watch the `max_steps` rate.

**Failure mode to mention:** a loop that varies one argument slightly each time (retrying a search with ever-so-different wording) evades an exact-match detector; the step and token caps are the backstop.

**60-90 second version:** "I use defence in depth. First, hard budgets in code: max steps, max tokens, wall-clock, and I check them before running the tools from a reply that blew the budget. Second, loop detection: a counter keyed on tool name and canonical arguments, so the third identical call stops the run, plus a circuit breaker on consecutive tool errors. Third, side effects: write tools are separate from read tools, run with least privilege, support dry-run and idempotency keys, have their own limits like a maximum refund, and anything irreversible needs human approval. Fourth, a trace for every run and alerts when the stop status is not done. The honest caveat is that detection by exact match misses near-duplicate loops, so the step and token caps are the real backstop."

**Follow-ups:**
- *How do you pick max_steps?* From traces: look at successful runs, take roughly the 99th percentile steps and add margin, then review the `max_steps` rate.
- *What about runaway cost across many runs?* Add per-user and per-day budgets at the gateway, separate from per-run limits.
- *Kill switch?* A flag checked each iteration (feature flag or per-tenant switch) so you can stop a misbehaving agent without a deploy.

## Q4 (extra). How do you test an agent deterministically?

**Define:** Separate the agent's control flow, which is code and can be tested exactly, from the model's judgement, which needs an evaluation set.

**Mechanism:** Inject the model as a dependency. A scripted fake returns canned replies; tests assert on statuses, tool calls made, messages the model saw, and side effects. Real-model quality is measured separately on a task set with trajectory and outcome checks.

**Decision:** Unit tests with fakes on every PR; eval sets on a schedule or before releases.

**Trade-off:** Fakes cannot tell you whether the real model picks the right tool; evals are noisy and cost money.

**Evidence:** My suite runs in milliseconds with no key. For model quality I would build a 30-50 task set with expected outcomes and tool-call checks.

**Failure mode to mention:** a fake model that is too cooperative, so the tests pass while the real model fails; keep a few recorded real transcripts as regression fixtures.

**60-90 second version:** "I make the model a constructor argument. In tests I pass a scripted model that returns pre-written replies, such as a bad tool call and then a corrected one, and assert on the loop's behaviour: it fed the validation error back, stopped at the budget, never ran the dangerous tool. That tests everything I own. What I cannot test that way is whether the real model chooses well, so I keep a separate eval set with expected outcomes and tool-call checks, and run it on a schedule."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Do you mock tools too?* Yes for unit tests; integration tests hit a sandbox or staging.
- *Flaky evals?* Run multiple samples per task and report pass rate, not a single pass/fail.

## Q5 (extra). When would you not use an agent?

**Define:** When the steps are known, the stakes are high and irreversible, or latency and cost must be predictable.

**Mechanism and decision:** If the flowchart exists, code it; use the model for the fuzzy substeps. If an action cannot be undone, make the model propose and deterministic code or a human dispose.

**Trade-off:** You give up the ability to handle unanticipated cases; you gain predictable behaviour.

**Evidence:** Say honestly which of your own projects were workflows and why.

**Failure mode to mention:** agent-by-default design that makes every simple request slow and expensive.

**60-90 second version:** "If I can write the steps down, I write them down. Agents earn their cost when the path depends on discoveries, like triage across systems. For irreversible actions I split decide from do: the model proposes, deterministic code validates, and a human approves above a threshold."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Hybrid?* Yes: a workflow whose single step is a bounded agent with its own budget.
- *How do you justify an agent to a sceptical lead?* Run both on a representative set and compare success, p95 latency and cost per task.

## Say-it-closed-book checklist

- Define agent vs workflow in one sentence each.
- Name the six stop statuses.
- Explain why limits belong in code.
- Give two loop-detection strategies and one weakness.
- Give three side-effect controls.
- State what you tested with a fake model and what you did not.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. The 'agent' was an unbounded loop that called search, then browse, then search again until the timeout. There was no tool schema, no token or step budget, and no stop condition besides the provider killing the request. State was the raw transcript. A calculator tool accepted a string and `eval`'d it. When asked the difference between an agent and a workflow the candidate said 'agents are smarter'.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'When is a workflow the better design?' Outline: the steps are known, the tools are few, and you want a testable path. Follow-up: 'How do you stop a runaway agent?' Answer: max steps, max tokens, a deny list of tools after N failures, and a human checkpoint before side effects.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut a second agent framework and an open-ended browse tool. Keep a schema, a budget, a stop rule, and one tool you can stub in a test.

lessons.title: Agent orchestration, durable graphs, MCP and approvals
lessons.summary: Stateful graphs with checkpoints and interrupts, durable execution, multi-agent trade-offs, MCP architecture and security, tool permissions and human approval gates.
keyPoints: A graph models a run as nodes, edges and persisted state; use it when you need pause/resume, human approval, restarts, explicit branching or an audit trail, not for short cheap runs.
Reducers define how node updates merge into state; a checkpointer saves state per step under a thread id, which enables resume, crash recovery and time travel.
On resume the interrupted node re-runs from its first line, so side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent (or moved to the next node).
Durable execution gives at-least-once step execution; use idempotency keys derived from business identity and save the next node before running it.
Multi-agent designs buy parallel breadth at a large token cost and add lossy handoffs; default to one agent or a workflow and prove the benefit on an eval set.

MCP standardises host/client/server communication (tools, resources, prompts over stdio or Streamable HTTP); it does not make servers trustworthy, so consent, validation, least privilege and untrusted-description handling remain yours.
Approve actions that are irreversible, high-impact or made after reading untrusted content; show exact arguments, bind approval to them, fail closed, and avoid approval fatigue.

check.q: In a LangGraph-style workflow, what happens to the paused node when you resume after an interrupt?
options: Execution continues from the line after interrupt() with the stack restored
The node runs again from its first line and interrupt() returns the resume value
Only the code after interrupt() is replayed
The graph restarts from the entry node
check.why: Checkpoints store state and the next node, not the call stack. The node re-executes from the top, so side effects placed before interrupt() repeat unless idempotent.

check.q: Which statement about MCP security is most accurate?
options: The protocol guarantees tool descriptions are safe, so clients can trust them
OAuth in the spec means servers no longer need to validate arguments
Tool descriptions, annotations and results from untrusted servers must be treated as untrusted; consent and validation stay with host and server
Using stdio transport removes the need for any security review
check.why: MCP standardises the wire format and auth flow, not trust. A malicious server can inject instructions via descriptions or results, and local servers run with the user's privileges.

check.q: A refund of 500 was approved by a human, but the model regenerates the arguments before execution. What is the right fix?
options: Execute the approved arguments stored in state, bound by hash, and refuse if they differ
Ask the model to be careful to reuse the same number
Lower the temperature to zero
Approve again automatically if the amounts look close
check.why: The approval must bind to the exact payload. Executing the stored, hashed arguments prevents a post-approval swap; prompting or temperature settings are not guarantees.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Stateful graphs, checkpoints, human approval, MCP concepts and tool permissions.
> **Prerequisites:** Agent fundamentals week.
> **Estimated time:** 50 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Agent workflow diagram + demo.

## Why a simple loop is not enough

Last week's agent loop keeps all state in one message list and runs in one process, start to finish. That breaks down when you need any of these:

- **Pause for a human** for hours or days, then continue exactly where you left off.
- **Survive a crash or deploy** in the middle of a run without redoing completed work.
- **Explicit control flow**: "after the lookup, go to approval only if the amount is above the limit".
- **Inspect, replay or fork** a run to debug it.

A **stateful graph** gives you that. You model the run as nodes (units of work), edges (what runs next), and a typed state object that every node reads and updates, and you persist the state after every step. Frameworks such as LangGraph package this; the GenAI End to End course, chapter 4 covers agent frameworks in general, so see the GenAI End to End course, chapter 4 for the wider landscape. This lesson teaches the concepts so you can explain them without a framework and map them onto one.

## Graph vocabulary (LangGraph-style)

| Concept | Meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **State** | A shared object (in LangGraph, a typed dict, dataclass or Pydantic model) that flows through the graph | Single source of truth for the run; must be serialisable to checkpoint it |
| **Node** | A function that reads state and returns a partial update | Unit of work and unit of retry |
| **Edge** | A fixed transition from one node to the next | Deterministic control flow |
| **Conditional edge** | A routing function that looks at state and returns the next node name | Branching, loops, "agent decides" |
| **Reducer** | A rule for merging a node's update into a state key (overwrite by default, or append, or merge) | Lets several nodes or parallel branches contribute to one key safely (for example a message list that appends) |
| **Checkpointer** | Persists a snapshot of state after each step, keyed by a thread id | Pause/resume, crash recovery, time travel, long-lived conversations |
| **Thread** | One logical run or conversation, identified by `thread_id` | The cursor you reuse to resume; a new id starts fresh |
| **Interrupt** | A node pauses the run and surfaces a payload to the caller | Human approval and input |

In LangGraph specifically (verify against current docs, since APIs evolve): you build a `StateGraph`, add nodes and edges, `compile()` it with a checkpointer, and invoke it with `{"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}`. A node calls `interrupt(payload)` to pause; you resume by invoking again with `Command(resume=value)` on the same thread, and that value becomes the return value of the `interrupt()` call. A checkpointer is required for interrupts. In-memory checkpointers lose state on restart, so production uses a database-backed one (the docs list Postgres and SQLite savers). Checkpointers (short-term, per thread) are distinct from stores (long-term, cross-thread memory).

### The rule that trips people up: resume re-runs the node

When you resume after an interrupt, the paused node runs again **from its first line**, and `interrupt()` now returns the human's answer instead of pausing. So any side effect placed before `interrupt()` in that node will happen twice. The LangGraph docs call out the same rules: do not wrap `interrupt()` in a bare try/except, do not reorder interrupt calls within a node, and make side effects before an interrupt idempotent. Practical advice: put the interrupt first, or give it its own node, and do the side effect in the next node.

## Durable execution

**Durable execution** means a run can be stopped at any point (crash, deploy, wait for a human) and resumed without losing completed work. The mechanism is: persist state at step boundaries, and on restart continue from the last checkpoint. Consequences you must design for:

1. **At-least-once step execution.** If the process dies after a node's side effect but before the checkpoint is written, that node will run again. Make side effects idempotent (idempotency key derived from business identity, such as `refund-<order_id>`, not a random id generated inside the node).
2. **Determinism around the checkpoint.** Do not branch on `now()` or random values in code that is replayed unless you store the value in state.
3. **State must be serialisable** (JSON-like), small, and versioned. When you change the state schema, old checkpoints still exist.
4. **Retention.** Checkpoints accumulate; prune them. Checkpoints can also contain personal data, so apply the same retention and access rules as the primary store.

Dedicated workflow engines (Temporal, for example) solve the same problem with different trade-offs; mention them as the heavyweight alternative when an interviewer asks about long-running business processes.

## When to use a graph instead of a plain agent loop

| Use a graph when | A plain loop is fine when |
|---|---|
| Humans approve steps, possibly after a long delay | The run finishes in seconds and nobody approves anything |
| The process must survive restarts | Losing a run is cheap, the user just retries |
| There are several distinct phases with different tools or prompts | One prompt and a handful of tools |
| You need branching, retries per node, or parallel fan-out and join | Linear tool use |
| You need an audit trail of every state transition | A log of tool calls is enough |
| Different teams own different steps | One developer owns the whole thing |

Cost of the graph: more code, a persistence layer to operate, state schema migrations, and harder local debugging. If you cannot name the specific capability (pause, resume, branch, replay) you need, stay with the loop.

## Multi-agent patterns, and when not to

Common shapes:

- **Orchestrator-workers:** a planner splits a task and delegates to workers, then merges results. Useful when subtasks are independent and large (parallel research).
- **Router / handoff:** a triage agent picks a specialist and hands over the conversation.
- **Pipeline:** specialist stages in sequence (extract, verify, draft). This is a workflow with model steps.
- **Critic / reviewer:** a second model checks the first's output.

**When not to:** most tasks that people split across agents are solved better by one agent with good tools, or by a workflow. Each extra agent adds model calls (cost, latency), a communication surface for errors and injection, and more states to test. Anthropic's write-up of its multi-agent research system reports that multi-agent runs used far more tokens than single-agent chat (consult the post for their exact figures); that is the right mental model: multi-agent buys breadth on parallelisable, high-value tasks and pays in tokens. A sceptical counterpoint widely cited is Cognition's "Don't build multi-agents", which argues that sharing full context between agents is hard and fragmented context causes conflicting decisions. A good interview answer names both.

Decision test: can the subtasks run independently, with small well-defined inputs and outputs? If yes, consider workers. If they need constant shared context, use one agent.

## MCP: what it standardizes

The **Model Context Protocol** is an open protocol, specified at modelcontextprotocol.io, that standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data. Without it, each app writes a custom integration for each tool (an N-by-M problem); with it, a tool is wrapped once as an MCP server and any MCP-capable host can use it.

### Architecture

- **Host:** the AI application the user runs (an IDE, a desktop assistant, your agent app). It owns the model connection, the user interface and the policy.
- **Client:** a connector inside the host that holds a one-to-one connection to one server.
- **Server:** a program that exposes capabilities.
- Messages are **JSON-RPC 2.0**.

### What a server can expose

| Primitive | Who controls it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Tools** | The model decides to call them (host may require approval) | `get_order_status`, `create_issue` |
| **Resources** | The application chooses what to attach | A file, a DB row, a doc, addressed by URI |
| **Prompts** | The user picks them (templates, slash commands) | "Summarise this PR" template |

Clients can offer features back to servers, such as **sampling** (the server asks the host's model for a completion, so the host stays in control of the model), **roots**, and **elicitation** (the server asks the user for input through the client). Tools carry a name, description and a JSON Schema `inputSchema`, and can have annotations such as read-only hints. The spec says annotations are hints and clients must not trust them from an untrusted server.

### Transports

- **stdio:** the host launches the server as a subprocess; newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout. Server logs must go to stderr, never stdout.
- **Streamable HTTP:** a remote server exposes an HTTP endpoint; this is the standard remote transport. The older HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated.

### Spec revisions: check which one you are on

The spec is versioned by date. As of this writing, published revisions include 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28. The 2025 revisions use an `initialize` / `notifications/initialized` handshake and, on HTTP, session ids. The 2026-07-28 revision (per its changelog) removes protocol-level sessions and the initialize handshake, adds `server/discover`, and moves per-request version and capability data into `_meta`. The worked example speaks the handshake-style revision; always check the revision your SDK and client negotiate. Client libraries (the official Python SDK, for instance) are the safe way to stay current, and their class names have changed between major versions, so read the SDK docs for the version you install.

### Authorization and security responsibilities

MCP standardises the **wire format and some of the auth flow**, not the safety of what happens behind it.

- **Remote servers** use OAuth-based authorization (the spec builds on OAuth 2.1 and metadata discovery; consult the authorization page for the current details). Local stdio servers typically use credentials from the environment instead.
- **What the protocol does not give you:** a trustworthy server, safe tool descriptions, safe tool outputs, or consent decisions.

Remaining responsibilities:

| Party | Must do |
|---|---|
| **Host / client** | Show users what a tool will do and obtain consent for risky calls; treat tool descriptions, annotations and outputs from untrusted servers as untrusted; validate inputs; keep per-server credentials separate; limit which servers and tools are enabled; log calls |
| **Server** | Authenticate and authorise every request against the end user; validate all arguments; apply least privilege to downstream systems; never pass through tokens meant for another service (the spec's security guidance calls this the token passthrough anti-pattern); defend against SSRF if it fetches URLs; rate limit |
| **Both** | Check Origin and bind local HTTP servers to localhost; avoid confused-deputy flows where a proxy server reuses one OAuth client id for many users without per-client consent |

Named risks from the MCP security guidance: confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF, session hijacking, and local server compromise (a malicious local server command runs with the user's privileges). There are also prompt-injection routes unique to tool ecosystems: a malicious server can put instructions in a tool **description**, and a poisoned tool **result** can steer the model. Treat every third-party MCP server like a third-party dependency with code-execution reach: pin, review, and sandbox it.

## Tool permission models

| Model | How it works | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Default deny allowlist** | Only listed tools can run | Production agents |
| **Per-tool mode** | allow / ask / deny per tool | Mixed read and write toolsets |
| **Parameterised rules** | "refund: ask when amount exceeds 50" | Business thresholds |
| **Scoped credentials** | Tool holds a token with only the needed scope | Limiting blast radius even if the agent is tricked |
| **Per-user authority** | Tool acts with the end user's permissions, not a god-mode service account | Multi-tenant apps |
| **Session grants** | User approves once for a time or scope window | Developer tools; risky if the window is wide |

Fail closed: if a rule cannot be evaluated (missing amount, unparseable value), deny or ask.

## When a human should approve an action

Ask on a combination of **irreversibility, blast radius and uncertainty**:

- Irreversible or hard to undo: sending email, deleting data, payments, production deploys.
- External effects on third parties.
- Value above a threshold, or access to sensitive data classes.
- Low model confidence, or the action was proposed after the agent read untrusted content.
- First time a new tool or server is used.

Do not ask for read-only, reversible, low-value actions: approval fatigue trains users to click yes, which defeats the gate. A good approval prompt shows the **exact action and arguments**, the **reason**, and the **effects**, and the approved payload is what executes (not a re-generated one: bind the approval to the arguments, otherwise the model can change them after approval).

## Trade-offs

- **Quality / safety vs latency:** every approval adds human wait time, which can be hours.
- **Cost:** checkpoints add storage and write latency per step; multi-agent multiplies tokens.
- **Complexity:** graphs need schema versioning and operational care.
- **Privacy:** checkpoints hold conversation data; encrypt, scope and expire them.
- **Reliability:** durable execution trades exactly-once fantasies for at-least-once reality plus idempotency.

## Common failure modes

1. Side effect before an interrupt runs twice on resume.
2. Approval granted for one payload, different payload executed.
3. State schema changed, old checkpoints fail to load.
4. Cyclic graph with no exit (always keep a step guard).
5. Approval fatigue from gating everything.
6. Trusting MCP tool descriptions or annotations from a server you do not control.
7. A multi-agent design where agents echo each other's mistakes.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The graph had no checkpoint, so a crash after the third tool call restarted from zero and re-sent an email. Human approval was a comment in the prompt ('ask if unsure'). MCP was described as 'like an API' with no mention of tool permissions or untrusted servers. The demo succeeded once on a happy path and had no replay. State lived in the model's head between turns.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'The process dies after a refund tool is chosen but before it runs. What happens on restart?' Outline: a checkpointed graph restores state, the refund node is idempotent, and approval is recorded as a durable event. Follow-up: 'What does MCP change?' Answer: a standard way to expose tools; you still decide which servers and which tools the agent may call.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a custom protocol and a second orchestration library. Keep a state diagram, one checkpoint, one approval node, and a permissioned tool list.

parts.body:
## What you are building

The proof artifact for the week is an **agent workflow diagram plus a working demo**. The demo here is a refund workflow with all the mechanics from the Concepts part, built by hand in about 130 lines so you see exactly what a framework gives you:

- Nodes, edges, conditional routing and **reducers** (the `log` key appends).
- A **JSON checkpoint** written atomically after every step, with history.
- An **interrupt** that pauses the run for human approval and **resumes in a fresh process** from the file.
- **Idempotent execution** so a crash between side effect and checkpoint cannot double-refund.
- A **tool permission policy** (default deny, ask above a threshold).
- A **minimal MCP server** at the protocol level, with tests.

Files (one folder): `graph.py`, `refund_flow.py`, `policy.py`, `mcp_min_server.py`, `test_orch.py`, `test_mcp.py`. Run with `pip install pytest` then `pytest -q` (expect 15 passed). No API key and no model are needed: the decision nodes are deterministic stand-ins. In a real system the `propose` node would call a model and validate its output; the orchestration around it is unchanged.

## Walkthrough: `graph.py`

- `Interrupt` is an exception; `Context.interrupt(payload)` raises it on the first pass and returns the resume value on the re-run. That is the same observable behaviour as LangGraph's `interrupt()`, including the re-run-from-the-top semantics.
- `JsonCheckpointStore` appends a checkpoint per step to `thread_id.json` and writes via temp file plus `os.replace`, so a crash never leaves a half-written file. Thread ids are restricted to alphanumerics, dash and underscore, because the id becomes a filename (a path traversal test pins this). The history list is what makes time travel possible: you can load any earlier checkpoint and fork from it.
- `Graph.run` loads the latest checkpoint (or creates one), then loops: run the node, merge the update through reducers, compute the next node (conditional router or fixed edge), **save a checkpoint with `next` pointing at the node about to run**. Saving `next` before running it is what makes crash recovery work: if the node dies, the checkpoint still says "next: execute".
- A resume value is passed only to the first node run after resume, then cleared.
- `max_steps` guards cyclic graphs.

## Walkthrough: `refund_flow.py`

Flow: `lookup` then `propose`, then a conditional edge: amounts up to 50 go straight to `execute`; above 50 go to `approve`, which interrupts. After approval the router goes to `execute` or `reject`. The `execute` node uses an idempotency key built from the order id and a `Ledger` that ignores a repeated key, mimicking a payments API with idempotency support.

Note the comment in `approve`: because the node re-runs on resume, nothing with side effects sits before `ctx.interrupt`.

## Walkthrough: `policy.py`

`decide(tool, args)` returns `allow`, `ask` or `deny`. Unknown tools are denied, thresholds are evaluated on typed values, and a non-numeric amount fails closed (a model might send the string "500"). In the graph version of an agent, an `ask` result routes to the approval node; a `deny` result becomes an error observation.

## Walkthrough: `mcp_min_server.py`

This is **protocol-level**, deliberately without an SDK, so you see the wire format: one JSON message per line on stdin, one reply per line on stdout.

- `initialize` returns the protocol version, the server capabilities (`tools`) and server info. `notifications/initialized` is a notification, so it gets no reply.
- `tools/list` returns each tool's `name`, `description` and `inputSchema`.
- `tools/call` returns `content` blocks and an `isError` flag. **Invalid arguments are a tool execution error** (`isError: true`) so the model can see the message and retry; an **unknown tool** is a JSON-RPC protocol error (`-32602`). Unknown methods return `-32601`.
- `handle()` is a pure function, which is why most of the tests need no subprocess; one test launches the real script and checks the reply count over stdio.

What it is not: it skips capability negotiation details, auth, pagination, logging and the other revision styles. It follows the 2025-style handshake; check the revision your client negotiates, since the 2026-07-28 revision drops the handshake. For a production server, use the official SDK for your language and its docs for the version you install, because the high-level Python API names have changed between major versions. The SDK derives the tool's `inputSchema` from type hints, which is what you would normally want.

## Walkthrough: tests

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| small refund straight through | Conditional edge skips approval |
| large refund pauses, nothing refunded | The side effect happens only after approval |
| resume in a fresh process | State really lives in the file, not memory |
| rejection | Reject path, no refund |
| resume without a decision | A missing answer does not advance the run |
| finished thread not re-executed | Calling `run` on a done thread is a no-op |
| crash after side effect | Idempotency key plus checkpoint-before-run gives exactly one refund |
| reducers | Append reducer and default overwrite |
| cycle guard | `max_steps` stops runaway graphs |
| history | Checkpoint sequence for time travel |
| thread id traversal | No path escape |
| policy | Default deny, thresholds, fail closed |
| MCP handshake, errors, stdio | The protocol shape above |

## The diagram deliverable

Draw the workflow as a Mermaid or whiteboard diagram with: nodes, conditional edges labelled with their conditions, the interrupt point, where checkpoints are written, and which nodes have side effects (mark them). Under it, write three lines: **what happens on crash**, **what happens if the human never answers** (add a timeout node that expires the thread), and **what is logged**.

## Exercises

1. Add an `expire` path: if no decision arrives within 24 hours, a scheduled job resumes with `{"approved": false, "reason": "timeout"}`.
2. Make `approve` bind the approval to the payload: store a hash of the proposal in the interrupt payload and have `execute` refuse to run if the proposal in state no longer matches.
3. Add a time-travel helper that forks a thread from checkpoint N under a new thread id.
4. Wire `policy.decide` into the loop from last week: `ask` routes to an interrupt, `deny` returns an error observation.
5. Add `resources/list` and `resources/read` to the MCP sketch for a read-only doc URI.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The graph had no checkpoint, so a crash after the third tool call restarted from zero and re-sent an email. Human approval was a comment in the prompt ('ask if unsure'). MCP was described as 'like an API' with no mention of tool permissions or untrusted servers. The demo succeeded once on a happy path and had no replay. State lived in the model's head between turns.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'The process dies after a refund tool is chosen but before it runs. What happens on restart?' Outline: a checkpointed graph restores state, the refund node is idempotent, and approval is recorded as a durable event. Follow-up: 'What does MCP change?' Answer: a standard way to expose tools; you still decide which servers and which tools the agent may call.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut a custom protocol and a second orchestration library. Keep a state diagram, one checkpoint, one approval node, and a permissioned tool list.

import pytest

from graph import END, Graph, JsonCheckpointStore
from policy import decide
from refund_flow import Ledger, build


@pytest.fixture
def store(tmp_path):
    return JsonCheckpointStore(tmp_path / "ckpt")


def test_small_refund_runs_straight_through(store):
    ledger = Ledger()
    result = build(ledger).run("t1", store, input={"order_id": "A100"})
    assert result.status == "done"
    assert ledger.refunds == {"refund-A100": 30}


def test_large_refund_pauses_and_nothing_is_refunded_yet(store):
    ledger = Ledger()
    result = build(ledger).run("t2", store, input={"order_id": "B200"})
    assert result.status == "interrupted"
    assert result.interrupt["proposal"] == {"action": "refund", "amount": 120}
    assert ledger.refunds == {}
    assert store.latest("t2")["status"] == "interrupted"


def test_resume_in_a_fresh_process_with_approval(tmp_path):
    ledger = Ledger()
    build(ledger).run("t3", JsonCheckpointStore(tmp_path), input={"order_id": "B200"})
    # simulate a restart: new store object, new graph object, same directory
    result = build(ledger).run("t3", JsonCheckpointStore(tmp_path), resume={"approved": True})
    assert result.status == "done"
    assert ledger.refunds == {"refund-B200": 120}
    assert result.state["log"][-2:] == ["approve: yes", "execute: refunded under key refund-B200"]


def test_rejection_issues_no_refund(store):
    ledger = Ledger()
    g = build(ledger)
    g.run("t4", store, input={"order_id": "B200"})
    result = g.run("t4", store, resume={"approved": False})
    assert result.status == "done" and ledger.refunds == {}
    assert result.state["log"][-1] == "reject: no refund issued"


def test_resume_without_a_decision_stays_paused(store):
    g = build(Ledger())
    g.run("t5", store, input={"order_id": "B200"})
    again = g.run("t5", store)  # no resume value supplied
    assert again.status == "interrupted"


def test_finished_thread_is_not_re_executed(store):
    ledger = Ledger()
    g = build(ledger)
    g.run("t6", store, input={"order_id": "A100"})
    n = len(store.history("t6"))
    assert g.run("t6", store).status == "done"
    assert len(store.history("t6")) == n and ledger.refunds == {"refund-A100": 30}


def test_crash_between_side_effect_and_checkpoint_is_safe_because_of_idempotency_key(store):
    class FlakyLedger(Ledger):
        fail_once = True

        def refund(self, key, amount):
            super().refund(key, amount)  # the money moved...
            if self.fail_once:
                self.fail_once = False
                raise ConnectionError("lost the response")  # ...but we never learned that

    ledger = FlakyLedger()
    g = build(ledger)
    with pytest.raises(ConnectionError):
        g.run("t7", store, input={"order_id": "A100"})
    assert store.latest("t7")["next"] == "execute"  # checkpoint still points at the failed node
    assert g.run("t7", store).status == "done"       # retry re-runs execute
    assert ledger.refunds == {"refund-A100": 30}     # exactly one refund


def test_reducers_accumulate_and_default_overwrites(store):
    g = Graph(reducers={"log": lambda old, new: (old or []) + new})
    g.add_node("a", lambda s, c: {"log": ["a"], "x": 1})
    g.add_node("b", lambda s, c: {"log": ["b"], "x": 2})
    g.add_edge("a", "b")
    result = g.run("t8", store, input={})
    assert result.state == {"log": ["a", "b"], "x": 2}


def test_cycle_without_exit_hits_the_step_guard(store):
    g = Graph(max_steps=5)
    g.add_node("a", lambda s, c: {})
    g.add_edge("a", "a")
    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="max_steps"):
        g.run("t9", store, input={})


def test_history_allows_time_travel(store):
    g = build(Ledger())
    g.run("t10", store, input={"order_id": "A100"})
    nodes = [c["next"] for c in store.history("t10")]
    assert nodes == ["lookup", "propose", "execute", END]


def test_thread_id_cannot_escape_the_directory(store):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        store.latest("../etc/passwd")


def test_policy_default_deny_and_threshold():
    assert decide("get_order", {}) == "allow"
    assert decide("rm_rf", {}) == "deny"
    assert decide("refund", {"amount": 20}) == "allow"
    assert decide("refund", {"amount": 500}) == "ask"
    assert decide("refund", {"amount": "500"}) == "deny"  # unparseable -> fail closed
    assert decide("delete_account", {}) == "ask"

import json
import subprocess
import sys

from mcp_min_server import handle


def test_mcp_handshake_list_and_call():
    init = handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": {}})
    assert init["result"]["capabilities"] == {"tools": {"listChanged": False}}
    assert handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}) is None
    tools = handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list"})["result"]["tools"]
    assert tools[0]["name"] == "get_order_status" and "inputSchema" in tools[0]
    ok = handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call",
                 "params": {"name": "get_order_status", "arguments": {"order_id": "A100"}}})
    assert ok["result"] == {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Order A100: shipped"}], "isError": False}


def test_mcp_error_kinds():
    bad_args = handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "tools/call",
                       "params": {"name": "get_order_status", "arguments": {"order_id": 7}}})
    assert bad_args["result"]["isError"] is True and "error" not in bad_args  # tool execution error
    unknown = handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "nope"}})
    assert unknown["error"]["code"] == -32602                                  # protocol error
    assert handle({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 6, "method": "bogus"})["error"]["code"] == -32601


def test_mcp_server_speaks_over_stdio():
    lines = [
        {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": {}},
        {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"},
        {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list"},
    ]
    proc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "mcp_min_server.py"], input="\n".join(map(json.dumps, lines)) + "\n",
                          capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
    replies = [json.loads(x) for x in proc.stdout.splitlines()]
    assert [r["id"] for r in replies] == [1, 2]  # no reply for the notification
